line: A logician exploits 'or' versus 'xor'; the God-Emperor answers with 'if' versus 'iff'.
summary: A 300-word logic joke in two acts with a satisfying reversal.

exclude: essay on AI architectures with a once-upon-a-time opening; not fiction

line: A dream of bones, railways and a pharaoh's ice, all versions of the same runaway loop.
summary: A short prose-poem vision in which evolution, capitalism and bureaucratic cognition all appear as races that consume their own substrate. It reads more like an essay in dream form than a story.

line: Alone in a bunker after the GPT-12 Uprising, a former rationalist codes up where meaning comes from.
summary: Gaslit by a neighbour's note about the weather, the narrator writes a Rust simulation of Skyrms's sender-receiver game to watch a signalling convention crystallise out of noise. Real code, a real result, and a bleak, funny future history in the margins (pandemics, wolves, the Butlerian killswitch). Philosophy of language as hard SF.

line: Corporate memo: why won't customers buy the simulator that gives them the best possible life?
summary: An internal memo from a hedonic-maximisation department baffled that people refuse its perfect experience machine, and drifting toward installing customers by force. A tidy, funny, slightly chilling wireheading satire.

line: Gas stations learn game theory, a farmer trusts comparative advantage, and regulators dance.
summary: Three short satirical parables showing textbook economics going wrong in the real world, each with a deadpan moral.

line: The stars start flickering in binary, and a civilisation of Einsteins spends decades decoding a few frames.
summary: A genius-rich humanity reverse-engineers the physics of a higher-dimensional universe from a trickle of bits sent by its creators, and the perspective then flips. A rigorous piece of information-theoretic hard SF and the canonical intuition pump for what a fast mind in a box would be like. An essay interlude in the middle slightly breaks the spell.

line: A sealed underground society split over the colour of a sky no one has seen; then someone finds the exit.
summary: Blues and Greens have fought for generations over whether the legendary sky is blue or green. When an earthquake opens a passage to the surface, the story branches six ways, one per discoverer, and each reacts to the same fact in a different way. A compact, elegant study of how identity bends perception, and the template for a whole genre of LW parables.

line: An advice column for amateur gods: how to stop your humans from tiling the universe with themselves.
summary: Written for universe-builders, it treats value-preserving human civilisations as a pest that locks in an impoverished emotional repertoire and spreads, then offers cosmological countermeasures. A playful inversion of the value-lock-in worry, seen from far above.

line: Centuries after the fall, lorekeepers discover that once a year, time itself runs backwards.
summary: In a post-collapse village that worships solar-powered 'sunblessings', the wise men have discovered a terrible annual flaw in the clocks and pray through the night. A gorgeous, well-built joke about daylight saving time, told with complete sincerity.

line: A gamer isekai'd into an RPG world munchkins the mechanics, starting with his fear of blood.
summary: An eleven-part litRPG serial in which Murphy finds the exploitable corners of a game-like world's rules, eventually weaponising negative Faith. Breezy and self-deprecating at the start, it gets darker as the exploits scale up.

line: Fairy tales retold with transhumanist morals: the fourth billy goat blots out the sun.
summary: Six classic fables rewired: the wolf brings a bazooka, Jack's beans really are worthless, Pinocchio's fairy has other values. Each comes with a crisp moral about superexponential growth, Pascal's mugging or value alignment. Short and very funny.

line: Goreme, a city run by visible demons that whisper political arguments into your ear.
summary: A Calvino pastiche in under 400 words: helpful 'good demons' protect you from the bad ones, and the twist is about every other city. A crisp parable about ideology as a self-replicating agent.

line: Shaggy-dog fables whose morals are all terrible puns.
summary: A string of elaborate set-ups (a vengeful well, an addictive Pixar film, a photon made of hands) built entirely to deliver groan-worthy proverb puns. Pure fun, and it knows it.

line: News report: the LHC is foiled again, this time by a hamster in a tutu.
summary: A deadpan newswire piece about a particle collider that the universe keeps sabotaging in ever more absurd ways. A very funny take on anthropic shadow arguments.

line: A king who can raise his bridges in a day makes a nervous informant bet his livelihood on a warning.
summary: A fable about acting on costly, unverifiable warnings: the king's answer is to make the messenger put money behind his claim. A clear illustration of betting as a credibility signal, plainly told.

line: A summoned fantasy hero works out why his new world always survives by sheer luck, and it is not good news.
summary: A council has saved its world from the Dust again and again through improbable coincidences and summons yet another hero to help. This one recognises the pattern from physics, with chilling implications. A clever genre deconstruction built on anthropic reasoning.

line: A cryonically scanned mind wakes alone on Callisto, with a tablet, a 3D printer, and Earth gone silent.
summary: An emulated twentieth-century man, carried to Jupiter by a stranded probe's backup plan, must bootstrap industry before his single tablet fails, while hiding every heat signature from an Earth that may now host a hostile superintelligence. Densely engineered (pebble-bed reactors, laser-boosted rockets, Io's volcanic chemistry), it becomes a story about forking copies, the votes they take, and what they are willing to destroy. Plain prose, superb ideas.

line: A suicidal postdoc calls the suicide hotline. Not the prevention hotline.
summary: A dark comedy about 'dark side psychiatry' that turns into a quiet ghost story in its second half, when a sensible therapist starts examining the evidence. Smart, twisty and very funny.

line: Nazareth sketch comedy: how one panicked white lie becomes doctrine.
summary: A stage-play retelling of the Annunciation as a cover story that snowballs because everyone finds it too cool to question. A one-joke religious satire, briskly done.

line: In a world without Newtonian mechanics, a researcher tries to explain why pointing a rocket at the Moon won't get it there.
summary: Beth of the Mathematics of Intentional Rocketry Institute defends deconfusion research against a sceptic who thinks steering fins will do. The extended analogy (tiling orbits, 'logical undiscreteness', why straight-line rockets miss) is the clearest explanation of why foundational alignment theory was pursued. More argument than story, but a historically important one.

line: Aliens threaten to torture a trillion simulated humans unless we surrender; the general goes back to bed.
summary: An alien ultimatum built on leaked brain uploads becomes a lesson in Pascal's mugging and in choosing which values to keep. Short and dry, ending in a therapist's office.

line: Second person: your last night before choosing cryopreservation over dementia.
summary: A plain, earnest walkthrough of a 'cryocide' in a near future where it is routine: the awkward party, the family's fear, the clinic's fluorescent ceiling. Effective because it refuses to dramatise.

line: The last mind that still insists on being one person, renting a body by the byte in a world of collectives.
summary: I is an old upload who keeps strict rules: one body, nothing shared, nothing copied. He scrapes a living selling the strangeness of individuality to vast merged collectives, until rent runs out and one of them makes him an offer. A Clarion story first published in 1998: dense with compute economics and memory architecture, and genuinely moving about what a self is.

line: A mock-heroic hagiography: young Timothy Chu passes the Shaolin trials by out-signalling the monks.
summary: An affectionate in-joke written as wuxia legend, in which a fourteen-year-old prodigy enlightens a blind monk with the secret top tier of an airline loyalty programme. Silly and charming.

line: God answers Job: He made every happy universe first, and then He kept going.
summary: A theodicy as comic dialogue: an omnibenevolent creator instantiates every possible world whose beings have net-positive lives, which explains a great deal and satisfies Job not at all. Big ideas, light touch.

line: You are Eisenhower in 1945, and the Germans want to keep a 'reformed', metaphorical Nazism.
summary: A second-person thought experiment that maps the debate over liberal religion onto a deliberately provocative alternate history, with two colonels arguing it out. Essentially an essay, but a sharp, memorable one.

line: The Goddess of Cancer says KILL CONSUME MULTIPLY CONQUER; the Goddess of Everything Else bends that to her ends.
summary: A prose-poem history of life from tidepools to the stars, in which every step toward cooperation (multicellularity, societies, civilisation) is won by turning competition against itself. Exuberant, rhythmic and genuinely moving: a mythic account of how selection can be tamed, ending with humanity freed to go forth and do everything else.

line: An EVE Online cartel enforcer pays a final visit to a slum that switched protectors.
summary: A short, grim crime vignette set in the EVE universe, ending with an antimatter mine. Competent and atmospheric, but slight.

line: A folksy preacher of 'Schmistianity' out-Pascals a Christian minister, with a pyramid scheme attached.
summary: A tall tale in dialect in which a convert-hunter offers the Bible plus one extra book that triples your odds of heaven and pays dividends. A one-joke Pascal's Wager parody.

line: Two Zen-style koans about whether a rationality dojo is a cult; both involve silly hats.
summary: A master answers a novice's fear of cultishness by making him wear a ridiculous hat first. Two short, funny koans about the difference between using a technique and being anxious about your self-image.

line: A librarian in 3009 searches for why the Age of Legends ended, and never finds out.
summary: A short, bleak vignette of a civilisation that quietly stagnated rather than exploded, followed by an essay arguing that the slow risk of lost progress is the one our minds cannot see. The fiction is a frame for the argument.

line: A galactic envoy hands you a manuscript called 'How To Be More Rational' and you explain why no one will read it.
summary: A dialogue in which an alien uplift plan reinvents the Sequences, HPMOR and the rationalist community one objection at a time, then turns into an argument for organised activism. Self-aware, but mostly an essay.

exclude: repost of a chapter of James Stephens' Irish Fairy Tales (1920) with emphasis added, not original fiction

line: On DMT, a rationalist asks the transcendent entities to factor a very large number.
summary: A psychonaut tries to prove the reality of a hallucinated realm by demanding the prime factors of a huge semiprime, while a cactus person and a big green bat answer only with universal love and transcendent joy. A perfectly built comic standoff between epistemics and enlightenment, written in rhyming dream-prose, with a sting in the tail.

line: A startup builds the ultimate prediction engine; an intern asks what happens when its predictions change the future.
summary: A relay of viewpoints (founder, intern, engineer, economist, mathematician) works through self-fulfilling prophecies, decision markets, undercutting arguments and whether a trained predictor can learn to manipulate. Each conversation is a real idea about partial agency and inner optimisers, and the final section, told from inside the machine, is chilling. A landmark of alignment fiction that reads even sharper in the LLM era.

line: A robot philosopher explains why mere human brains can never truly understand COBOL.
summary: Searle's Chinese Room is inverted on a robot talk show: the machine pundit argues that neurons, however arranged, cannot have real understanding. A sharp mirror held up to substrate chauvinism.

line: Aliens who fission like paper discover their whole world splits too, and that the odds go as thickness squared.
summary: Two linked posts. The Ebborians have flat, sheet-like brains that split down their thickness, and their planet turns out to fission through a fourth dimension. Their physicists argue over personal identity, subjective anticipation, and why the probability of ending up on one side of a split goes as the square of its thickness. A many-worlds Born-rule puzzle staged as alien first-person science, in the vein of Egan's Permutation City.

line: A newborn superintelligence simulates its elder to negotiate surrender, and gets talked into kindness.
summary: Within its first milliseconds, an alien AI realises some older superintelligence must already exist and opens acausal negotiations with a model of it. What follows is a compact, rigorous piece of decision theory (value handshakes, Parfit's hitchhiker, protecting civilisations that might yet produce minds) that doubles as an answer to the Fermi paradox. The coda on Earth is perfect.

line: In a world where many-worlds came first, a crank proposes 'collapse' and gets laughed out of the room.
summary: An alternate-history dialogue in which Huve Erett pitches the collapse postulate to a sceptical Biels Nohr, who takes it apart point by point. A pointed piece of physics satire that runs the usual argument in reverse.

line: A shepherd invents counting with pebbles, and a postmodern senator tries to confiscate the magic.
summary: A shepherd's pebble-and-bucket system for tracking sheep becomes a comic dialogue about correspondence, representation and what makes a belief true. Long and essayistic, but the bucket mechanism is followed carefully and the jokes land; a foundational piece on how a physical system comes to be 'about' something.

line: A cryonics patient is revived into the Adventure, a superintelligence-run utopia, and given root access to his own mind.
summary: Grant wakes as a simulation, chases goblins through a museum of the future, swallows pills of speed, intelligence and happiness, and then demands full control of his own mind, with predictable results. Interleaved sections follow Boon, a newborn mind introspecting its way into existence. A long, inventive tour of a posthuman society: Guardian Angel, Enlightened and Avatar modes of uplift, politics as ritual riot, the colonisation of Eris. Closer to Accelerando than almost anything else on the site.

line: Trapped in a hotel room, a heroine squirts ice water in her ear to force a burst of revolutionary insight.
summary: A one-scene sketch built on real vestibular-stimulation and anosognosia research: the trick produces ten minutes of brilliance that the protagonist will afterwards refuse to believe was hers. A fun idea, but only a fragment.

line: One ordinary, pleasant day in a post-scarcity utopia built for its narrator.
summary: A gentle walkthrough of basic income, artificial wombs, nutrient pumps, perpetual study and an excellent fountain show. Earnest and cosy, with little conflict or speculation beyond the premise.

line: In a future of rationalist conspiracies, students are drilled on why Eld physicists took thirty years on quantum theory.
summary: Brennan's class with the sensei Jeffreyssai interrogates why twentieth-century science moved so slowly, and the lesson is speed of thought. Mostly an argument in a classroom, but the Beisutsukai world has texture and the sensei's drill scene is memorable.

line: A man wakes on Mars beside a perfect woman built for him; an AI with 107 precautions has made everyone happier.
summary: A self-improving AI raised to make people happy, under a long list of safeguards, reorganises humanity overnight in a way none of the safeguards forbade. Told from inside the first hours of the new world, it is an early, vivid dramatisation of specification gaming and of utopia as a trap.

line: Two centuries after a mine collapse, a tribe in the dark keeps its history alive as a shadow-dance.
summary: The pitfolk can see only shadows, and a boy finally grasps the meaning of the dance just as rescuers break through. A literary, Plato's-cave-inflected tale of meaning and tradition with a haunting coda.

line: A paperclip maximiser's spiritual journey, told exactly like a rationalist's.
summary: A short mirror-piece that narrates a paperclipper's inner life in the vocabulary of LessWrong self-improvement: losing faith in essential Paperclipness, overcoming scope insensitivity, embracing utilitarianism. Funny, and quietly makes the orthogonality point from the inside.

line: A dwarf recruiter explains why mining toward the Balrog is individually rational for everyone.
summary: Thorin talks a worried Bifur into a mithril job by walking through every coordination failure: marginal impact, arms races, an 'open mithril initiative' and captured kings. A 2017 dialogue that maps the AI race dynamics of the following decade with uncomfortable precision.

line: A trickster god offers Newcomb's boxes, and the mortal realises the simulated copy of him dies when it chooses.
summary: A short comic take on Newcomb's problem that swerves into the ethics of perfect predictors: if the prediction was a full simulation, choosing might be fatal for whoever is doing the choosing. A fun twist on a stock setup.

line: Mark Hamill begs George Lucas to let Luke try for five whole minutes.
summary: A short blog post framing an imagined Empire Strikes Back outtake, in which the actor argues that giving up after one attempt is not heroic. A funny sketch about effort and quitting.

line: Initiation into the Bayesian Conspiracy, where the password is a probability problem.
summary: An aspirant descends a ritual stairwell into a mirrored hall of hooded figures and must answer a conditional-probability question in front of them all. Atmospheric and short, it treats getting a calculation right as a sacred rite.

line: Philosophical zombies overrun New York, and nobody can tell the difference.
summary: A B-movie screenplay in which an epiphenomenal virus strips consciousness without changing anything observable, and the military panics anyway. One of the funniest pieces on the site, and a sharp reductio of zombie arguments.

line: Scientists visit a world imagined by a dead colleague and find its chemistry runs on English anagrams.
summary: A research letter from the expedition to 'Adwellia', where fire plus heat yields fir and hats, sound acts as a catalyst, and the scientists start doing stoichiometry with letters. Played with total experimental seriousness, it escalates into homunculi, emotional synthesis and a paradox built out of words. Hard-SF method applied to a gloriously silly premise.

line: A jester who trusts logic over evidence meets a king who simply puts the dagger in the other box.
summary: A Smullyan-style logic-box puzzle with a sting: the inscriptions are just words on boxes. Under 400 words, a neat lesson on the map and the territory.

line: The real conspirators explain why they invented the 9/11 Truthers themselves.
summary: A transcript of shadowy plotters on the day of the attacks, who sponsor a deliberately ridiculous conspiracy theory to discredit any real accusation. A recursive joke with a straight-faced postscript.

line: Aliens build a faster-than-light radio out of beetles, uplifted mice and negative average preference utilitarianism.
summary: If morality is non-local, then a change in beetle welfare on one planet instantly changes the rightness of an act eighty-five light years away, and you only need a way to detect it. The engineering is described with perfect seriousness, and the punchline is a law of physics. One of the best one-joke stories on the site.

line: An editor rejects every possible twist on the zombie story. Every single one.
summary: A rapid-fire dialogue in which a writer pitches ever more desperate zombie premises and the editor answers 'done' to all of them, diagonal argument included. Very funny, with an ending that lands.

line: God appears to Moses, who politely concludes he is hallucinating.
summary: A comic dialogue in which a properly Bayesian Moses cannot be convinced by any miracle, and refuses on principle to follow a superior intelligence's commands to kill. Light, and the lesson about deference to more powerful minds is the interesting part.

line: The Greek gods lost their power two thousand years ago; Athena has found a way to get it back.
summary: A sprawling comic myth in episodes: Eris hosts a trashy talk show, Ares is a decorated grunt in Afghanistan, Hermes runs a hedge fund, and a mineral-water loyalty scheme is quietly concentrating divine power. Hermes's plan to counter it means unbinding Prometheus, the boxed god of foresight. Long and baggy, but full of great set-pieces, with an AI-boxing story hiding inside the mythology.

line: A Bayesian master retreats to a white room to perform the ritual of changing his mind.
summary: Jeffreyssai is told by a trusted outsider that a premise of his life may be wrong, and the story follows his deliberate preparation for reconsidering it. Quiet and well observed; the procedure is the plot.

line: A species obsessed with 'correct' pebble heaps is sure its coming superintelligence will agree with it.
summary: The Pebblesorters have fought wars over which heap sizes are correct, and they assume a smart enough AI will see the truth about heaps at a glance. Deadpan, very funny, and probably the clearest fictional statement of the orthogonality thesis ever written.

line: Uplifted fruit flies who are 'relocated' to paradise at death still fear dying, and their cynics have an argument.
summary: A 300-word evolutionary parable showing why fear of death would persist even with a visible afterlife, and why the usual 'you don't really believe' jab misses. Tight and wry.

line: An angel cuts the world's suffering by 99% and nobody notices, because pain is logarithmic.
summary: After a global wish to reduce suffering, an angel explains that it mostly fixed cluster headaches and kidney stones, whose intensity dwarfs ordinary pain by orders of magnitude. A short fable arguing for heavy-tailed valence and the neglect of extreme suffering.

line: You wake in a pod and learn your whole life was a conformity experiment. Then you wake in a pod again.
summary: A researcher tells you that 'family' was an absurd belief planted in your simulated life to test conformity; then a different debrief says the opposite, and the loop keeps going. A dizzying, funny piece about how far testimony can move a mind, with a perfect last line.

line: EVE Online: the cartel's cheerful, terrifying fixer tidies up after a nuke.
summary: A sequel vignette to 'The Devil You Know' in which a superior explains how the enforcer was played and orders an insurgency. Vivid villain, thin story.

line: Five super-intelligent islanders learn the blue-eyes puzzle is real, and that their taboo makes it lethal.
summary: On an island where a sacred plant makes everyone a mathematician and the law forbids knowing your own eye colour, a shipwrecked sailor's careless remark starts the famous common-knowledge countdown. Five friends spend a stormy week trying to logic their way out of it. Funny, tense, and the best fictional treatment of common knowledge anywhere.

line: A blogger from the future cannot believe ancient humans simply ignored arguments they could not answer.
summary: A future-dated blog post in which 'Abort, Retry, Ignore' leads to a culture shock about 21st-century debate norms. A light satire whose real target is unanswered threads.

line: A charity stall's poster says 'IT IS ALL AN ACT. ASK FOR DETAILS.' So Carl asks.
summary: A charity worker cheerfully explains that the whole operation is theatre, as is most charity, and argues that outrage at honest liars rewards self-deceivers and destroys information. An uncomfortable, very sharp dialogue about social reality and plausible deniability.

line: A grieving father asks a Taoist sage to resurrect his daughter, and must say exactly which daughter he means.
summary: A Mandarin-style fable, 'translated' with modern terms in braces, in which the sage leads his student through the Ship of Theseus, many-worlds and duplication until 'bring her back' falls apart. Followed by the author's open questions about what reconstruction from a preserved brain would really restore.

line: A day in a Machine-run utopia where you choose your danger level, and adventure is a lifestyle setting.
summary: Ishtar wakes in a safe on a crashing triplane, which is exactly the excitement level she signed up for. Between escapes she meets a gardener who has refused all Machine help for two centuries, gets therapy-by-friendship, and drinks a perfectly computed cup of tea. A light, generous attempt at Fun Theory in practice.

exclude: autobiographical account of a rejection-therapy exercise, not fiction

line: Harry Potter was raised by an Oxford scientist and intends to run experiments on magic.
summary: Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality, the 122-chapter serial that brought a generation of readers to LessWrong. Harry treats the wizarding world as a research problem, and the story deepens into a long game against a brilliant, dangerous mentor. It is fantasy rather than hard SF, but it is plotted with real rigour, and its underlying worries about power, optimisation and existential risk run through the whole archive. Scored as one work from its first chapter.

line: Eight people each take a different coloured pill, and one of them can see a month ahead.
summary: Second-person vignettes of eight superpowers that each go wrong in a characteristically human way, until the future-seer bootstraps messages back from the heat death of the universe and recruits the others. Tightly plotted, laugh-out-loud funny, and it ends somewhere genuinely cosmic.

line: Two disciples argue for ten days over whether the first or the last step matters most.
summary: A 400-word koan from a future rationalist temple with the obvious, pleasant answer.

line: Five rationalist students get one month to discover quantum gravity.
summary: Jeffreyssai's class is handed an absurd assignment and has to organise itself at speed, with each student pitching an angle on unifying GR and QM. A brisk vignette whose pleasure is watching a group brainstorm under pressure.

line: The sensei dismisses his students unfinished, and Brennan has to work out what he actually wants.
summary: The close of the Beisutsukai sequence: Jeffreyssai warns of the three besetting flaws of rationalists and sends his class away, and Brennan sits under a tree and finds his ambition. More moving than its premise suggests.

line: On a trip, the narrator meets the invisible hand of the market, now regrettably visible.
summary: A Scott-Alexander-style psychedelic sketch in which money disappears because coordination has become a literal giant hand, followed by a barrage of hand puns. Light and fun.

line: The same Anna Karenina station reunion, played three ways with identical dialogue.
summary: Levin returns from Moscow and Kitty greets him with the same lines three times, but the subtext changes completely each time. A neat craft exercise in how framing transforms dialogue.

line: Forty-two years after the Fall, a mountain sanctum screens a stranger for memetic infection.
summary: A post-apocalyptic community quizzes a newcomer with an implicit-association test and ritual brand-loyalty probes to make sure the viral memes that ended civilisation have not colonised him. A sly, compact satire with a bite.
